webTitle: US House ethics panel recommends censure for Republican Chuck Edwards

fields.headline: US House ethics panel recommends censure for Republican Chuck Edwards
fields.trailText: North Carolina congressman’s campaign rejects committee finding that Edwards ‘engaged in sexual harassment’
fields.bodyText: The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, they determined there “was substantial reason to believe” Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior likely violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. “A member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person’s appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers,” they continued. Edwards’s re-election campaign criticized the report, arguing its findings “completely exonerate” the congressman while saying ethics committee staff “have taken it upon themselves to write their own rules based upon an interpretation that is inconsistent with the written rule of law or House rules”. “Representative Edwards looks forward to having his name cleared and will work to ensure that the full light of day is brought on this process and that every member of Congress and the public can see the attempt to harm the congressman who has brought no harm to others,” the campaign said in a statement. If the House agrees to censure Edwards, he would have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The congressman was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up” in a sign of improving Democratic chances. “My heart goes out to the young women who took these roles to serve our community,” Jamie Ager, his Democratic opponent, said following the report’s release. “We deserve leaders with the moral character western North Carolina can be proud of.” Elected in 2022 after ousting the scandal-plagued Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary, Edwards, a former state senator, left most of the hiring for his new office up to his chief of staff, but insisted on bringing “three young women” into his operation, according to the report. This group included a woman who was still in college and identified by the committee as “Staffer 1” and a second woman in her early 20s, identified as “Staffer 2”. “Both young women were subject to increasingly unusual attention from the congressman while they worked for him, creating an environment where both they and their coworkers felt uncomfortable,” the committee found. These behaviors included Edwards bringing Staffer 1 to a White House event without telling the rest of his staff, buying her flowers and texting her in advance that he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted it to be “perfect”. After the event, the staffer said Edwards tried to “pressure” her into continuing the night together, which the congressman told the committee he did not recall. He invited both staffers to private dinners, and at one point told Staffer 2 to ensure the event was not put on his calendar by his office scheduler. He would also send both “personal texts” later in the evening about planning events together or expressing “personal sentiments”, the committee found. Edwards also planned lengthy and elaborate trips with the two staffers either together or individually, at one point suggesting to Staffer 2 that they “go to Annapolis for lunch, meditate by its water, stroll about town, find a day spa, see a movie, or wipe out the casino”. “I’m probably over thinking being impulsive but I really want you to enjoy our time together nearly as much as [I] know [I] will,” he wrote in a text message to the staffer released by the committee. His actions made the two staff members uncomfortable, and when a senior employee of his office spoke to Edwards on their behalf, that staffer told the committee the congressman “got very angry” and said she “didn’t understand the unique relationship” he had with the two women. Both staffers later resigned because of his behavior, but gave Edwards other reasons why when they departed. The behavior affected the morale of his office, the committee found, with one senior aide telling investigators Edwards “lashes out at everyone on the team except” the two women. The congressman denied yelling at his staff. Another staffer said they had told Edwards that an “unfair standard existed” in his office, which he said was caused by employees being “jealous”. Even after she left his employment, Staffer 2 agreed to a trip to Las Vegas with Edwards, saying she felt pressured to do so in part because he had influence over her being hired for another job in civil service. He paid for her flights, accommodation at the Bellagio hotel and a show at the Sphere. After receiving a bouquet of flowers upon arrival, Staffer 2 texted Edwards: “I’m almost ready and just got the flowers – they’re very pretty. Thank you! I did want to flag that the message made me uncomfortable. Just want to make sure this trip isn’t meant to be anything it’s not?” “Understood, and agree. I’m sorry it made you uncomfortable. Nothing was meant by it, other than what was intended to be a cute play on the name of the arrangement,” Edwards responded.

webTitle: Trump claims strait of Hormuz could open ‘by tomorrow’ as Iran denies any talks taking place – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump claims strait of Hormuz could open ‘by tomorrow’ as Iran denies any talks taking place – as it happened
fields.trailText: US president claims talks are ‘not very complex’ as he speaks at White House as Iran’s foreign ministry says there are no talks taking place with US
fields.bodyText: New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday. It comes a day after the US president again said he had called off further “massive strikes” because Gulf allies had urged diplomacy. It’s all very consistent with Trump’s repeated pattern over the last five months as he struggles to find an off-ramp; he threatens devastating military action, only to pull back at the last minute and claim the two sides are on the brink of an agreement to end the war. As my colleague Patrick Wintour notes, this is thought to be the 12th time in the war that Trump has called off threatened strikes. Indeed, Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme. “The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearization,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.” He also reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran, saying “this the last chance for them to sign a good document.” However, Tehran had on Monday denied that talks with the US were taking place. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters at a weekly press briefing on Monday that Iran is not currently holding any talks with the US – contradicting claims made by Trump on Sunday night that talks with Iran would happen the next day. Baghaei said that there were no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one, and that Iran’s current focus was on negotiations with Oman over the strait of Hormuz. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview with Iranian state television. To that, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media. He wrote on Truth Social: “They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’.” The Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor, the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself. As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week, Iran has shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party. But as soon as his latest attempt to hammer out a peace deal was announced, it was denied by Iran and the US president was left fuming once again. Trump has suggested dozens of times since the beginning of the war that a deal with Iran is imminent, and his latest claim that new negotiations could produce a peace deal within days has shown the administration’s desperation to reopen the strait and find a road map out of the crisis. After promising to hit Iran “very hard”, Trump made a U-turn on Sunday and claimed that talks would continue and that the “perimeters of a deal” for the opening of Hormuz and the “denuclearization of Iran” had been agreed. Unfortunately, the Iranians don’t agree. In a statement on Monday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson denied any peace negotiations were taking place. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” said Esmaeil Baqaei. “Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the strait of Hormuz.” That may result in an agreement. But that will not result in the return of the strait of Hormuz to its prewar status, Baqaei added, in effect keeping the waterway a political football for the foreseeable future. “We must ensure that the strait of Hormuz cannot be misused by parties that have committed aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei. Little has changed since the last round of negotiations. Iran remains capable of closing the strait of Hormuz and stifling shipping – including a fifth of global oil supply – through the crucial waterway. The US remains capable of inflicting devastating strikes on Iran – despite a shortage of key munitions that could be needed for a war against key rivals like China – but has a lack of meaningful targets that could force Iran to change its policy. The Trump administration has been signalling a desire to end the conflict since April and three ceasefires have come and collapsed since then. With just over three months left until the US midterm elections, in which the Republicans are expected to lose the House and possibly even the Senate, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll last week showed that fewer than a third of Americans support the war in Iran, and 69% believe that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran”. For Iran, the strategic unpredictability has become a new weapon in a war that has counterintuitively strengthened its negotiating position, giving the regime new tools in slowing global oil supply and in attacking regional US allies in the Gulf. Iran has concluded that its best strategy is to “maximise the pain that they can impose on the United States and its partners in the region”, said Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and an expert on Middle East security issues with a focus on Iran, during the institute’s podcast last week. The view there was that Trump “is not really yet ready for a deal with Iran, not a deal that would work for the Iranians anyway”. Iran is also facing a time crunch with a US blockade in effect halting trade out of the country. “They are now at a point where they don’t think just sitting back and having one round after another of diplomatic talks is the best way forward,” he added. “They’re trying to shake things up to try get Trump’s attention and see if they can get a different result.” Speaking in the Oval Office earlier, Trump also said that major oil companies are making “too much money” due to high prices stemming from his war on Iran, as he seeks to address his party’s political vulnerability ahead of the US midterm elections in November. “I don’t like it. They’re making too much money, okay? Based on a shortage, they’re making too much money. I don’t like it, and I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy,” he said. “Nobody bigger, and you know, you’re going to see oil when we’re finished with Iran. You’re going to see the prices drop through the floor. But they made too much money, too much money. Chevron, too much money. Exxon Mobil, too much, too much money.” High gasoline prices are a key political issue for Trump as his Republican Party heads into the midterms, with Democrats seeking to wrest control of Congress from them. The average price of a gallon of regular gasoline in the United States is up more than 37% since the start of the war, launched by Trump and Israel in late February. The war has seen Iran’s retaliatory action target Washington’s allies in the Gulf and virtually block the vital strait of Hormuz, with both moves sending energy prices skyrocketing. US petroleum giants ExxonMobil and Chevron released blowout profits on Friday, reflecting a major lift from the war that easily offset negative effects at both companies. ExxonMobil’s second-quarter profits more than doubled to $14.5bn, while Chevron’s came in at $12.1bn, more than five times the level in the year-ago quarter. Other major oil companies have also reported massive profits on the back of the war. Trump, a strong supporter of fossil fuel interests, has lashed out over prices at the pump, announcing in June that he was directing the US Department of Justice to investigate any “gouging” perpetrated by the industry. On Monday, he slammed the oil companies for their profits, saying he was “not happy about it”: When you look at one company where they made 12 times what they made the year before, they ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price. Too much money. You surprised I’m saying it. I’ll say it loud and clear. I’m not happy about it. With Agence-France Press. Donald Trump also said that newly planned talks with Tehran – which again, Iran has denied – are the “last chance” for Tehran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country. The US president reiterated that he’s running out of patience, telling reporters: We are talking right now [with Iran] at the request of Iran, backed by Saudi Arabia, backed by the UAE, and backed by Qatar in particular, but others also. Many countries called … but if it doesn’t happen, this is the last chance for them to sign a good document. Earlier, Trump also claimed – as he has in the past – that it was Iran who made contact with his administration to relaunch peace talks. He said: They called me and they said, please don’t attack. We’ll make a deal. That’s the real truth. And everyone knows it. And who wouldn’t call? One journalist in the Oval Office asked Trump what was different about this pause in airstrikes to previous occasions. Here was his response: I think we’re going to maybe get something, but I want to give them every last chance before decapitation. It’s very tough to do what I – what we – have planned. Still planned. We’ll see what happens. But it’s very, very tough thing to do. I think, I’m very proud of the fact that … I’ll give people a chance. Trump said allowing Iran to charge a toll on ships passing through the strait of Hormuz was not on the negotiating table. “I’m not going to let them charge anybody,” he said. “We have total control. You know, we have a thing called a blockade with the US Navy.” Donald Trump is speaking at an executive order signing at the White House, where he was asked where direct talks with Iran would take place. “You’ll find out today or tomorrow,” he said. “They’re going to go quickly one way or the other. It’s not very complex.” Trump said the strait of Hormuz could be open “literally by tomorrow”. “The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he said. “That’ll take a little while, but … we’re very strong on it.” Staying in Islamabad, Pakistani government sources have told Turkish news agency AA that intermediaries were yet to confirm a date or venue for the resumption of stalled negotiations between the US and Iran. No direct talks were scheduled in Pakistan’s capital in the next 24 hours, the agency reported. Donald Trump earlier insisted direct negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday afternoon. Mediators from Pakistan and Qatar are in contact with both Washington and Tehran, AA reported, with Islamabad and Doha likely venues for the proposed talks. A senior Pakistani official with direct knowledge of contacts between Islamabad, Washington, and Tehran told the Guardian over a phone on Monday that despite the current impasse, Pakistan remains actively engaged in quiet diplomacy aimed at reducing tensions between the US and Iran, insisting that Islamabad’s offer to help facilitate dialogue between the two sides “is still intact”. “We are actively involved in efforts to resolve US-Iran tensions,” the official said. “Our offer to facilitate contacts has not changed. The understanding reached earlier remains intact, and we continue to engage both sides.” The official said Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, has remained in close contact with senior US officials, including vice-president JD Vance and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff, as part of efforts to prevent further escalation in the region. “Field Marshal Asim Munir has been in contact with JD Vance and Steve Witkoff,” the official said. “These have been substantive discussions focused on regional stability and de-escalation.” At the same time, the official said Islamabad has maintained high-level communication with Tehran, including hours-long talks between Munir and Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi. “There have also been hours-long discussions with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi,” the official said. “Pakistan has channels open with both Washington and Tehran and believes dialogue remains the only viable path to avoid a wider regional conflict.” The official declined to disclose details of the exchanges but said Pakistan sees itself as one of the few countries maintaining the confidence of both capitals, allowing it to quietly encourage diplomatic engagement at a time of heightened regional tensions. Despite Trump insisting that talks with Iran began on Monday afternoon, officials tell CBS News there’s nothing new to announce after all, just the same negotiations, run through mediators by envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Donald Trump has lashed out after Iran denied it was in negotiations with the United States, declaring in an angry social media post that a US military blockade will continue until there is a “Deal, or Total surrender.” Calling Iranian leaders “duplicitous” for “openly and proudly” saying Iran was not negotiating, Trump wrote: “Whether Iran wants to admit it or not, we are, in fact, talking of a solution to a problem that they have caused, for decades.” The US president wrote on his Truth Social platform: Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous! They ask for a meeting, some would say “beg,” talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with “Oman.” They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, the Strait of Hormuz will be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our “Blockade” or, as some say, “The United States Wall of Steel!” Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished. Whether Iran wants to admit it or not, we are, in fact, talking of a solution to a problem that they have caused, for decades. It is very simple, IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON! People walk near a billboard depicting Iran’s late supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on a street in Tehran, Iran, earlier today. Six Saudi-flagged supertankers have changed course in the Gulf of Aden in recent days amid threats from the Iran-aligned Houthis, Reuters reports. The tankers, which were empty of cargo after returning from destinations in Asia, opted to avoid transit through the southern Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint by sailing in formation toward southern Africa, according to automatic identification systems data collected by Reuters. The Houthis of Yemen, who control the capital Sana’a and much of its Red Sea coastline, announced on 20 July that they were implementing a blockade against Saudi ships. They have since claimed to have been behind a number of strikes on Saudi tankers. Earlier today, Esmail Baghaei, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said that Iran was not reviving talks with the US – despite what Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday. However, Iran is continuing talks with Oman over the strait of Hormuz. The Guardian’s Patrick Wintour has the full story here: Crude oil prices fell sharply and European stock markets rallied on Monday after Donald Trump cancelled planned strikes on Iran to focus on negotiations for a peace deal. Brent crude was trading 5% lower at $83.50 a barrel by mid-morning, after falling as low as $81.55 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate dropped more than $5 to $79.47 a barrel. Both global oil benchmarks jumped more than 20% in July after fighting between the US and Iran resumed, and as attacks on several tankers in the strait of Hormuz revived fears for the safety of vessels transiting the important shipping passage. Michel Issa, the US ambassador to Lebanon, said on Monday that he was “encouraged” that the US-brokered peace talks between Israel and Lebanon are ongoing in Rome. “A great deal of technical work remains to ensure civilian safety on the ground. There is a meaningful difference between drafting an agreement on paper and implementing it responsibly — moving too quickly risks jeopardizing the very civilians this process is meant to protect,” Issa said in a statement. The ambassador continued: “We believe it is better to take the time needed to get this right the first time. Doing so will allow subsequent pilot zones to move forward more efficiently. Above all, both sides must agree on a clear, workable process before proceeding.” CNN reports that an officer in the intelligence branch of the US Central Command sent a message to a broad group of military analysts “looking for new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The email went out on Wednesday, before Donald Trump threatened to launch new strikes against Iran and then backed down after speaking on the phone to the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman. Iranian state media is reporting that Iran executed two people on Monday on charges of espionage and ⁠cooperation with Israel, according to Reuters. Omid Behzad and ⁠Pouria Safvat were accused ⁠of sending Israel the coordinates of military and security sites in addition to images and information in the latest conflict that began 28 February as well as during the brief war last summer, judiciary news outlet Mizan reported. A source briefed ‌on Israel’s military strategy told Reuters in March that Israel targeted checkpoints manned by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps during the current conflict based on intelligence from informants on the ground. Iran has executed at least 50 p[eople in the past four months on vague national security charges, including several 18- and 19-year-olds, Human Rights Watch reported last month. In January, Iranian authorities quelled a period of nationwide ⁠unrest by killing thousands of protesters. Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency reports that Israeli forces dropped phosphorus shells overnight in the towns of Yaroun and Haroun and the city of Bint Jbeil, sparking fires in olive and pine groves. International humanitarian law currently restricts the usage of white phosphorus, given its incendiary nature, according to Amnesty International. Though it can be used lawfully, it must never be fired at, or in close proximity to, a populated civilian area or civilian infrastructure. The IDF did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In addition to the phosphorus shells, Israeli forces also conducted an airstrike just after 1 a.m. local time Monday on the outskirts of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, according to the National News agency. An Israeli drone also dropped a sound bomb on Bouyout al-Sayyad, the news agency reported. Two ⁠tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb strait over the weekend, data collected by Reuters showed on Monday, despite the maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia declared by the Iran-aligned Houthis at the end of last month. Kpler data showed that 18 commodity vessels total passed the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Sunday, down from the 27 that passed on Saturday and the 28 on Friday. Two tankers – the Suezmax tanker Lesvos, carrying 1 million barrels of Saudi crude. and Very Large Crude Carrier Desh Vaibhav, 1 million barrels of Saudi crude – exited the Red Sea with ‌their automatic identification systems (AIS) transponders switched off, the data showed. The Houthis of Yemen, who control the capital Sana’a and much of its Red Sea coastline, announced on 20 July that they were implementing a blockade against Saudi ships, opening a new front against the US and its allies in the war on Iran. They have since claimed to have been behind a number of strikes on Saudi tankers. Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the Middle East. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters at a weekly press briefing on Monday that Iran is not currently holding any talks with the US, Reuters reports – contradicting claims made by Donald Trump on Sunday night that talks with Iran would happen the next day. Baghaei said that there were no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one, and that Iran’s current focus was on negotiations with Oman over the strait of Hormuz. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview with Iranian state television. On Sunday, Trump told reporters on Air Force One that he decided to hold off on ordering American forces to carry out new strikes against Iran at the urging of Gulf allies Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, including a phone call with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. “I said to the crown prince, ‘What would you rather do? Would you rather us do this or not?’” Trump said. “They said we would much prefer a deal as opposed to an attack, because you don’t know where these attacks lead.”

webTitle: Author of Democrats’ 2024 election autopsy report says chapter was left out

fields.headline: Author of Democrats’ 2024 election autopsy report says chapter was left out
fields.trailText: Paul Rivera says missing section included questions on Biden’s decision to run for re-election, the Times reports
fields.bodyText: The author of an infamous internal Democratic party report on the 2024 presidential election loss has claimed that an entire section that included a discussion of generational wealth established by high-ranking elected officials was cut from the draft version leaked and later released earlier this summer. Paul Rivera, the author of the autopsy, told the New York Times that a section titled “What Happened in 2024” was missing from the published version but had been included in the version he personally handed to embattled party chairman, Ken Martin, in January. The Democratic National Committee has previously claimed the autopsy had been released “in its entirety”. Rivera said that elements of the report that were excised included questions about Joe Biden’s decision to run for re-election and the policy influence of Democratic party operatives who had become “generationally wealthy off politics”. While the chapter did not name those who had become enriched he wrote that Democrats seeking change “keep banging their heads up against a system proven to be inflexible and self-enriching. “Whether that was a conscious decision on their part to bury the section for the purposes of hiding a paragraph, I don’t know,” Rivera told the Times. “That’s a them question. What I can tell you is they had it, and they made a decision not to release it.” Martin disputed that account in statement to the paper, saying “this alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed”. Had it been included, he added, “we would have released it with the rest of the report.” The report was released in May to resounding disappointment that it had failed to address why the party, or its two presidential candidates, Biden and later Vice-President Kamala Harris, had failed to gain sufficient traction to win against Donald Trump. The missing chapter, provided by Rivera and published in full by the Times, states that Democratic wins before the election led the party “to believe they were stronger than they actually were. President Biden, seeing those results, made the consequential decision to seek re-election even when Americans were already sending a very strong signal: they were unhappy with the status quo.” The report said that Democrats had failed to do enough to convince voters that Trump was an unacceptable candidate and made wrong assumptions about Latino and male voters. It pointed to successful Democratic candidates in swing states who concentrated on economic and cost-of-living messaging more than identity politics. The Democratic party now heads into the midterm elections in November and the 2028 presidential election with a significant $2m cash deficit while the Republican party nationally reports a positive balance over $128m. A recent supreme court decision indicates that the cash gap could widen. Among the topics Rivera attempted to address in the disputed “What Happened” chapter were entries about Biden’s decision to seek re-election; a loss of support among Hispanic, Black, Asian American and Native American voters; and the issue of party officials and consultants being insulated or divorced from voters’ concerns by wealth. “It is therefore possible the people ‘in the room’ at the highest levels of 2024 decision making misunderstood the mood and practicalities facing everyday America,” Rivera wrote, according to the missing section. “They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation.” The Times report may now set off a new round of questions about its direction as Democratic primary voters head to the polls in Michigan on Tuesday to choose between moderate and progressive Senate candidates Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Martin said the party would have released the disputed or missing chapter “that went after self-enriching consultants” if it had had them and that he personally had campaigned for the party chairmanship “to hold the consultant-industrial complex accountable and ensure the party only pays for work that actually helps us win”. Rivera said he was now going public with the claim, along with his own 564-page review of the election loss. “It’s coming from a place of hope and, honestly, a little bit of desperation,” he told the outlet. “I think that we need some disruption here to force change.”

webTitle: Will Missouri be the next primary win for a democratic socialist challenger?

fields.headline: Will Missouri be the next primary win for a democratic socialist challenger?
fields.trailText: Voters face a choice of progressive ex-congresswoman Cori Bush or pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday
fields.bodyText: The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton, has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza. “As a pastor who’s had eight members murdered, violence over there is terrible,” Burton said of the conflict in the Middle East. “We have to deal with the problems right in our metropolitan area,” Burton added. “While there’s kinship and stuff … you’re talking about blood overseas, blood on the TV. We got blood right here in our metropolitan area.” In Tuesday’s Democratic congressional primary, voters in Missouri’s deep-blue first congressional district will decide whether to give pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell a second term, or replace him with Cori Bush, a former progressive congresswoman who accuses Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza. Along with a heated primary in Michigan, the contest has become a proxy battle over the Democratic party’s role in supporting Israel’s military before the November midterm elections, which will determine which party holds the majority in both chambers of Congress. After losing to Bell two years ago, Bush, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is vying for her seat back, and a Super Pac linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) has so far spent more than $3m to try to keep her out. In recent weeks, Democratic voters in New York City and Denver ousted incumbents in favor of candidates who promised they would take a hard line against support for Israel. In Congress, large shares of Democrats have voted for unsuccessful efforts to block arms sales to the country’s security forces, and progressives hope that a win by Bush will underscore their movement’s momentum. “I think her victory this cycle would be monumental,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for Justice Democrats, which has long supported Bush and backed several of the other insurgents who ousted Democrats in recent primaries, though it is not channeling funds into the campaign this year. “We haven’t had a lot of cycles to try this out, but this would be the first time that we would be able to take a seat back from Aipac after they bought one and deliver it back to working-class people.” African Americans make up about half of the district’s population, and Burton said some draw parallels between their history in the United States, and how Palestinians have been treated in Israel. Others’ views have been affected by conflicts with Palestinian shopowners in predominantly Black neighborhoods, said Burton, who hopes that whoever wins does not forget the community’s needs. “It’s caused a level of divisiveness that really we don’t need in our community, in the light of what the African American community is dealing with, with the Trump administration and the various policies. We really don’t need these type of hard divisions and bitter feelings,” Burton said. Ubiquitous ads Elected in 2020 after beating long-serving incumbent William Lacy Clay, Bush was a member of “the Squad”, the informal grouping of progressive lawmakers of color that also included congresswomen Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar. Following the 7 October attack, Bush was one of the earliest and most forceful objectors in Congress against Israel’s counterattack in Gaza, staking positions on which many other Democrats were hesitant to join even as it became clear that Joe Biden’s support for Israel was complicating both his and, later, Kamala Harris’s campaign to keep Donald Trump out of power. It also put her in the crosshairs of Aipac, with the group and its allies spending heavily to unseat both Bush and New York Democratic congressman Jamaal Bowman. In an interview, Bush said their defeats changed how her party thought about Israel, and how they voted on issues like the Massie amendment, a recent proposal in the House of Representatives to block some military aid to Israel that failed, but only after receiving votes from nearly half of the Democratic caucus. “If Jamaal and I would still be in Congress, we’d still be voting no on some of these bills, and … people would just be going on as if Aipac was not still influencing elections,” Bush said. “I credit the fact that we didn’t stop, that we grew the coalition, and then having the loss grew the coalition even more.” Bell and Bush can both trace their political journeys to the unrest in the St Louis suburb of Ferguson following the 2014 police killing of Michael Brown. Bush was an activist in the protests that followed, while Bell unseated the longtime St Louis county prosecutor after promising voters he would reopen the case of the police officer who killed Brown, but ultimately decided not to charge him. “The people in St Louis, they want someone that cares,” said Maria Miller, a Democratic candidate for state legislature who met Bush during the protests in Ferguson. “And once you betray them from that trust, it becomes like a war, because they’re very combative, and I just don’t feel that Wesley Bell’s earned that trust.” Though international conflict overshadows the race, both candidates have made prominent campaign promises to counter Trump, help the city and county recover from a deadly tornado last year and reverse years of divestment and high crime. While polling in the race is scarce, Bell is the clear leader in fundraising, having brought in $3.5m, for his own campaign in addition to the support from the Aipac-linked Super Pac United Democracy Project. Ads from his campaign and his supporters are ubiquitous in the district, with Bell making his case that Bush was an ineffective lawmaker, citing her no vote on Biden’s 2021 infrastructure legislation, as well as a comment where she appeared to accuse both Biden and Harris of “fascism”. Bush has responded that she voted against the infrastructure bill because it did not include additional social spending Biden had promised voters, and that the “fascism” comment was taken out of context. Each candidate has accused the other of corruption, with Bush noting protesters arrested at a town hall the congressman held last year have sued him and his security guards for allegedly assaulting them. Bell has seized on reports that Bush is paying her husband with campaign funds to provide security, and noted the justice department investigated her while she was in Congress. She has denied any wrongdoing. In an interview, Bell emphasized he could not coordinate or control the spending by outside Pacs. He describes Israel as an ally worth supporting alongside Ukraine, Taiwan and western Europe, and said he opposed the Massie amendment as “more of a show, as opposed to serious public policy”. “I’m not a fan of Netanyahu, but I think it’s important to stand with all of our allies,” he said. Bell rejected the idea that the trends that unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette in Denver, or Adriano Espaillat in New York, chair of the congressional Hispanic caucus, would oust him next: “What happens in New York is not the same as what’s on the ground in Texas, is not the same as what’s happening in Wisconsin, and it’s not the same in St Louis.” Sean Fauss, the chair of St Louis City Democrats, acknowledged the potency of concerns about Israel, but said Bush had made significant errors during her two terms. “I have my differences with Congressman Bell on that very issue,” Fauss said of the congressman’s views on Israel. “But I’m not going to support a candidate who made speaker Pelosi have to count on Republican votes in order to get President Biden’s infrastructure bill across the line, and that’s what Cori Bush did.” Russell Gunn, a Democratic former state lawmaker who is supporting neither candidate, warned that the Aipac-linked spending was “a liability” for Bell because of the controversy surrounding it. “But I don’t think it’s a big enough liability that he’s going to lose the election,” he said. “It helps him in some areas, and it hurts him in others.” ‘Because of Trump’ Bush’s campaign has raised a comparatively small $1.3m, and is going without the assistance of Justice Democrats’ Pac, which spent $2m trying to keep her in office in 2024. Andrabi said the group’s “limited set of resources” and long list of candidates it is backing has kept it from spending on Bush. On an uncomfortably hot afternoon, 22-year-old Alec Martirez joined a small group of volunteers for Bush who went knocking at the doors of voters in the leafy suburb of Maplewood, which had only recently been added to the district after Missouri’s Republican leaders redrew their maps to oust the state’s only other House Democrat. A former co-chair of the Young Democratic Socialists of America at the University of Missouri, Martirez had hosted Bush on the campus, and was drawn to her views on Israel after watching the invasion of Gaza play out over social media. “I just thought that was unacceptable that somewhere halfway across the world there was a genocide taking place with money that I was giving my federal government here,” he said. A few days prior, Bush and Bell had met for a combative debate on St Louis Public Radio, where Bell had pressed his challenger on the allegations of financial mismanagement. When Martirez knocked on the door of a white brick home, the woman who answered said she’d watched the encounter hoping to hear an explanation from Bush. “She didn’t satisfy my concerns and I’m pretty sensitive about that right now because of Trump,” said the woman, who did not want to give her name but said she had cast an early ballot for Bell. The views were reversed further down the block, when Katie Davies, 44, emerged on to her porch and declared she was ready to vote for Bush, saying she didn’t feel Bell had done enough to help the city recover from the tornado and found Aipac’s involvement in the district’s politics unseemly. “Blind support for Aipac candidates is not leading us to anything,” she said. As he walked away, Martirez pulled up an app on his phone that allowed him to track which houses he had visited and how they were leaning. “I think I’ll mark her down as a supporter,” he said.

webTitle: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring? | Jan-Werner Müller

fields.headline: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring?
fields.trailText: The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
fields.bodyText: The pattern is by now all too familiar: with every power grab Trump tries – from a fraudulent speech about voter fraud to appeals to his supreme court to let him rig the midterms – a debate kicks off about whether these moves are signs of strength or of desperation. Maybe we keep getting caught in this debate because the question is badly posed. So much of what is distinctive about Trump’s governance during his second term can serve the consolidation of an autocratic regime and at the same time create particular vulnerabilities for the regime. We have to become better at identifying these weaknesses, as opposed to being shellshocked by Trump’s brazenness every single time. Aspiring autocrats operate differently in the 21st century; in previous eras, they had little hesitation about unleashing violence and committing massive human rights violations. Today, they try to fool both domestic and international audiences into thinking that democracy and the rule of law still exist. The recently deposed Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orbán, was a master of this technique; he spent many years performing what he called “the peacock dance” to convince the European Commission (and Chancellor Angela Merkel) that he wasn’t creating a kleptocratic autocracy. This contrast between what the social scientists Serguei Guriev and Daniel Treisman have called “fear dictatorships” on the one hand and “spin dictatorships” on the other is empirically proven: there really is less violence, according to Guriev and Treisman, than in the 20th century. But elaborate efforts to fake democracy do not change the fact that violence is always kept in reserve: Putin dropped the mask entirely in 2022 and now has no hesitation to be seen as the violence-prone dictator who in one sense he always was. It is crucial to understand how Trump differs from these patterns: unlike Orbán, for instance, he was never constrained by international institutions and other powerful capitals (let alone “international public opinion” – even mentioning the term in as self-centered a country as the US seems faintly ridiculous). What’s more, his own modus operandi, from his early days as a New York real estate investor onwards, has always been to simply do things that everyone can see are illegal – the point is to create facts on the ground (think of the demolition of the East Wing) and hope that the other side will settle out of court or just live with a fait accompli. This method (strategy might be too big of a word) of illegality – and hope for impunity – now characterizes almost the entire administration. More particularly, the Trumpists have figured out that a scandal per year can spell political death, while 10 scandals a day elicit hardly a shrug, because no one, it seems, can keep up. This “flooding the zone” with scandals is in itself a means of generating power – but it also creates vulnerabilities. One never knows whether one scandal – even a relatively harmless one like the reflecting pool disaster, combining grift and incompetence – might not focus the public’s attention after all and become a symbol for the corruption of the regime as a whole, the way that one child abuse scandal – an Orbán ally pardoned a man convicted of covering up abuse – became the symbol of everything wrong with Orbán’s rule. Every aspiring autocrat faces a trade-off between loyalty and competence. It is no secret where Trumpists have tended to be placed on the spectrum. That total devotion to the leader – including the willingness to lie shamelessly, or at least engage in election denial, as a de facto loyalty oath to Trump sworn in public – can consolidate power. But it also creates a distinct vulnerability, as, sooner or later, the egregiously incompetent will produce terrible outcomes, plain for all to see (at least if an effective opposition party manages to make them plain to see). Contrary to the tendency of today’s dictators shying away from violence – so as not needlessly to invoke memories of 20th-century authoritarianism and provoke resistance – Trumpists have made a spectacle of cruelty. Again, this can contribute to consolidating power – after all, the glaring impunity apparently enjoyed by the men who killed Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero sends a signal that loyalists can count themselves above the law. The spectacle might also please a Maga audience. But the fact is that, in the end, the ostentatious displays of cruelty have not been popular with the public at large. For now, the administration increases its power by effectively telling people “We can do whatever we want, and you can’t do anything!” But making cruelty a priority also creates images that can be turned against it. And the shameless corruption? Again, the shamelessness might easily generate a sense of hopelessness on the part of Americans watching unprecedented acts of malfeasance. But, unlike with other aspiring autocrats, the Trumpists are not really creating a coherent system of self-enrichment (the way Orbán did with what came to be called his mafia state – where tricks with public procurement were disguised well enough for many years). Under Trump, everyone just grabs whatever they can as quickly as they can. That inability to build a system is ultimately a sign of weakness; the Trumpists themselves do not really seem to believe that their rule will last, and what Mike Johnson, in a revealing moment, called the Republicans’ “protection program” – the majority in Congress – might be gone this year. Self-confident creators of autocratic kleptocracy would have stayed silent on the point – and been smarter in their approach altogether. To be sure, that is no consolation for victims of cruelty. Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University
